505.title: The woman no one could see
505.hook: an empty hermitage, a curse, and the way back built into it
505.carry: prayashchitta: penance, and a way back
505.howItsDone: Ahalya is honored in Hindu tradition as one of the panchakanya, five women whose names some Hindus recite in a well-known morning verse; her story is told very differently across tellings, and discussions of it often turn on those differences.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Siddhashrama: Maricha hurled over the sea, alive, and the sacred fire kept burning to the end. Your line was guard the yajna, the sacred fire.

With the sacrifice done, the hermits at Siddhashrama have a plan. King Janaka of Mithila is holding a great sacrifice, they tell Rama, and he keeps a bow there you should see. So they walk north for days, and every evening the sage tells stories: how the Ganga came down from heaven, how the ocean was churned. Just outside Mithila, they pass an old hermitage. Lovely, but completely empty. No smoke from the fire, no voices. Whose was this, Rama asks, and why is no one here?
screen: `NORTH, TOWARD MITHILA.` → `STORIES EVERY EVENING.` → `AN EMPTY HERMITAGE.`

segments.voice: This was the hermitage of the great sage Gautama, Vishvamitra tells him, and his wife Ahalya. One day, while Gautama was away, Indra, king of the gods, came to Ahalya disguised as her husband. Here the versions part, and it matters which you're hearing. In Valmiki's telling, Ahalya sees through the disguise and agrees anyway, out of curiosity about the king of the gods. Some later tellings say she was fully deceived. Either way, Gautama comes home, sees Indra slipping out in the sage's own form, and curses them both. To Ahalya he says: you will stay here for thousands of years, unseen by any living being, living on air, lying in ash, doing penance. And in the same breath: when Rama comes and you welcome him as a guest, you'll be free. Here's the Hindu teaching tucked inside. The tradition has a word for it: prayashchitta, penance, atonement. A wrong has real consequences; that's karma. But in Hindu teaching a consequence isn't the end of a person. Penance works it through, and the way back is part of the story from the start. Ahalya's years in the ash aren't wasted. They're her tapas, and tomorrow you'll see them make her shine. And here's what surprises people. Some Hindus, as part of their morning prayers, recite a short verse remembering five honored women, the panchakanya. The first name in it is Ahalya. Not hidden away. Remembered first. So the empty hermitage isn't empty. Someone has been there the whole time, doing her penance, waiting for a guest. Go in, Vishvamitra tells Rama. Tomorrow, what happens when he does.
screen: `GAUTAMA, AHALYA, AND INDRA.` · `THE VERSIONS PART.` · `UNSEEN, UNTIL RAMA COMES.` · `PRAYASHCHITTA: PENANCE, AND A WAY BACK.` · `HER YEARS IN THE ASH: TAPAS.` · then, large: `AHALYA, REMEMBERED FIRST.`

segments.voice: If you pray, you can do what some Hindus do each morning and say the five names slowly: Ahalya, Draupadi, Sita, Tara, Mandodari. If you don't, think of someone paying a long time for a mistake, maybe yourself. Don't retell the mistake. Just picture the way back already open, and on each breath out let a little warmth go their way.
Ahalya restored. Gautama's wife, doing penance unseen until Rama comes, and remembered first among five honored women.
Your line: prayashchitta, penance, and a way back. Even Gautama's curse named its own end. Until tomorrow.

506.title: Ahalya, seen at last
506.hook: she isn't stone in Valmiki, and two princes bow at her feet
506.carry: touching feet: honoring the sacred in someone
506.howItsDone: In much of popular Hindu tradition, Ahalya is freed from stone by the touch of Rama's foot, a scene loved for what it says about Rama's grace; Valmiki's version, where she is invisible and freed by hosting him, is often taught alongside it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ahalya restored, part one: an empty hermitage, a curse, years of penance, and a way back built in. Your line was prayashchitta, penance, and a way back.

On television, in comic books, from a grandmother's lap, the scene usually goes like this. A stone lies by the path. Rama's foot brushes it, and the stone becomes a woman. It's a beautiful picture, and an old one. But it isn't Valmiki's. In Valmiki's Sanskrit there's no stone at all, and no foot brushing against one. What happens instead is quieter, in some ways more striking, and it starts with a woman nobody can see.
screen: `A STONE BY THE PATH.` → `RAMA'S FOOT TOUCHES IT.` → `NOT IN VALMIKI.`

segments.voice: Rama walks into the hermitage, with Vishvamitra and Lakshmana behind him, and there she is. Ahalya, shining with the power of her long penance, the text says, but hidden: like a flame wrapped in smoke, like the moon behind a cloud. Until now, no one could see her at all. Now Rama sees her, and the curse is over. Then the brothers take hold of Ahalya's feet, the respect you'd show an elder. Two princes, one of them the prince Hindus worship as Vishnu come to earth, bow at the feet of a woman the world has looked away from for years. She remembers Gautama's words and receives them as guests, with water for their feet and honor. Flowers fall from the sky. Gautama returns, and they're together again. Now the version most people grew up with, from later tellings like Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas: Ahalya as a stone, freed by the touch of Rama's foot. Two tellings, and both turn on feet. That's no accident in Hinduism. Touching the feet, charan sparsh, is how Hindus honor a parent, a grandparent, a teacher, a saint, or God's image, and ask for a blessing. Devotees long for the dust of the Lord's feet. Many teachers read the gesture as bowing to the sacred in that person. In Tulsidas, grace flows from Rama's foot to the stone. In Valmiki it flows the other way too: the prince people worship bows first, at her feet. The honor goes both ways. That's why, before an exam, a trip or a wedding, you'll see Hindu kids bend to a grandparent's feet, and a hand come down on their heads in blessing.

507.title: The daughter of the furrow
507.hook: a priest asks about his mother, and a king tells where his bow, and his daughter, came from
507.carry: bhumi devi: the earth is a mother
507.howItsDone: Hindus celebrate Sita's appearance from the earth on Sita Navami, in the month of Vaishakha, and Mithila, in today's Bihar and Nepal's Janakpur region, holds her as its own daughter. Many Hindus also greet the earth on waking with a short Sanskrit verse asking her pardon for the touch of their feet.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ahalya restored, part two: no stone in Valmiki, and two princes bowing at her feet. Your line was touching feet, honoring the sacred in someone.

The travelers reach Mithila, and King Janaka comes out to receive them with his priests. One is Shatananda, Janaka's chief priest. His first question to Vishvamitra isn't about the bow, or the princes, or the sacrifice. Did you show my mother to Rama? Was she honored? Did my father come back to her? Shatananda is Ahalya and Gautama's eldest son. Yesterday's story was his family's. And when he hears yes, she's free, they're together, he's overjoyed. Then the king speaks of something else.
screen: `MITHILA, AND ITS PRIEST.` → `DID YOU SHOW MY MOTHER TO RAMA?` → `YES. SHE'S FREE.`

segments.voice: These boys would like to see the bow, Vishvamitra says, and Janaka tells its story. Long ago, at the great sacrifice of Daksha, Shiva was refused his share of the offerings, and in anger he raised this very bow against the gods. They begged him to relent; he did, and gave them the bow, and the gods gave it to Devarata, an ancestor of Janaka's line. It has stayed in Mithila ever since. Then Janaka tells a second story, about his daughter. Once, he says, I was plowing a field to prepare for a sacrifice, and out of the furrow the plow had cut, a girl rose up. I raised her as my own and named her Sita. Sita means furrow, the line a plow cuts. She wasn't born from a womb, the text says; she came from the earth itself. That's why she's called Bhumija, daughter of the earth. And here is the teaching under the story. Hindus honor the earth as a goddess, Bhudevi or Bhumi Devi, a mother who feeds and holds everyone. Sita is her daughter, and at the very end of the Ramayana, she goes home to her. So this isn't a humble birth. It's the most sacred one in the story. That's why many Hindus, on waking, touch the floor before stepping on it and ask Mother Earth to forgive the touch of their feet. And Janaka has decided: only the one who can handle Shiva's bow may marry this daughter of the earth. Tomorrow, what that has cost him.

508.title: The kings who couldn't lose
508.hook: kings who couldn't lift it decided to take Mithila instead
508.carry: ahamkara: the ego that can't bear to fail
508.howItsDone: Across India, the contest of the bow is staged in Ramlila performances; later retellings such as the Ramcharitmanas present it as a swayamvara, while Valmiki describes Sita as viryashulka, won by strength.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the daughter of the furrow: Shiva's bow from Daksha's rite, and Sita, found in the earth. Your line was bhumi devi, the earth is a mother.
screen: `BHUMI DEVI: THE EARTH IS A MOTHER.`

segments.voice: Janaka made a decision about his daughter, and he announced it. Sita, he said, is viryashulka: the price of her hand is strength. Not gold, not alliances, not land. Whoever can lift and string Shiva's bow may marry her. Word spread. Kings came from everywhere to try, and every one of them failed. Then, Janaka tells Vishvamitra, something ugly happened. Wounded pride doesn't always go home quietly. Sometimes it comes back with an army.
screen: `THE PRICE OF HER HAND: STRENGTH.` → `KINGS COME FROM EVERYWHERE.` → `EVERY ONE OF THEM FAILS.`

segments.voice: The kings who failed were furious, insulted by a bow. They joined forces and laid siege to Mithila, and for a whole year the city was surrounded and supplies ran low. Janaka couldn't match their armies. So he turned to austerity and prayer, and the gods answered him with an army of their own. The kings were scattered and fled. Hindu teaching has a name for what drove those kings: ahamkara. Literally, the I-maker. It's the part of us that says: this is about me, my name, my standing. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna traces how a mind fixed on itself goes wrong, one step at a time. Dwelling on something breeds clinging, clinging breeds wanting, wanting breeds anger, and anger clouds the mind. That's the siege, step by step. The kings didn't really lose a bride; they lost face, and ahamkara can't bear that. Now look at Janaka. No army, no way to win, and still he keeps his word: strength earns his daughter, not force. He sets down his own pride and turns to the gods. That's the spirit behind a small ritual you'll see at temples. Many Hindus break a coconut before God, and families often explain it this way: the hard shell is the ego, cracked open so what's sweet inside can be offered. So when Janaka finally shows Rama the bow, it's no party trick. It arrives in an iron chest on an eight-wheeled cart, hauled in, the text says, by five thousand strong men. The whole hall waits to see what the young prince will do.
screen: `THE KINGS FAIL, AND BESIEGE MITHILA.` · `AHAMKARA: THE I-MAKER.` · `CLINGING, WANTING, ANGER.` · `JANAKA KEEPS HIS WORD.` · `THE COCONUT: A SHELL CRACKED OPEN.` · then, large: `THE HALL WAITS.`

segments.voice: Remember a time something didn't go your way in front of others, and feel where the sting lands. That's ahamkara, the I-maker. Don't fight it. On each breath out, picture it as a hard shell cracking a little, like a coconut offered at a temple. If you pray, offer the sting to God. If you don't, let the memory sit there, smaller.

509.title: Lifted as if in play
509.hook: a bow no king could lift, picked up as if it were nothing, and the sound that follows
509.carry: lila: what crushes kings is God's play
509.howItsDone: The breaking of the bow is a high point of Ramlila performances and Ramayana recitations; in many places audiences cheer as the bow snaps, and the scene is often painted and sung at weddings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Janaka's bow, part two: kings who failed the test and besieged Mithila. Your line was ahamkara, the ego that can't bear to fail.

The chest is open. The bow lies there, enormous. Nobody in the hall speaks. Vishvamitra looks at Rama and says one short line: Rama, my son, look at the bow. No speech. Rama steps forward and asks, politely: may I touch it? May I try to lift it, and string it? The king and the sage both say yes. And then, in front of thousands of people, something happens that Valmiki tells in only a few verses.
screen: `RAMA, LOOK AT THE BOW.` → `MAY I TOUCH IT?` → `THEY BOTH SAY YES.`

segments.voice: Rama takes hold of the bow in the middle and lifts it, the text says, as if in play: the bow thousands of men just dragged in on a cart, the one a line of kings couldn't budge. He bends it and strings it. He draws the string back, all the way to his ear. And with a crack like thunder, the bow breaks in two. The earth shakes. Everyone in the hall falls to the ground, stunned, except four: Vishvamitra, King Janaka, Rama and Lakshmana. Notice first that Rama asked before he touched it. No grabbing, no pride; that was yesterday's kings. Then notice that phrase, as if in play. Later devotees heard a whole teaching in it: lila, divine play. In Hindu thought, God doesn't act out of need or strain. The world itself is often called God's lila, done freely and with joy, the way a child plays. What crushes kings is play for the Lord. That's why the plays that act out Rama's life every autumn, around Dussehra, are called Ramlila: Rama's play. In towns and temples people stage this very scene, and crowds cheer when the bow snaps. When the people come to, Janaka is full of joy. I've seen Rama's strength with my own eyes, he says. Sita will bring glory to our family by marrying him. My promise is fulfilled. He sends fast messengers to Ayodhya to bring King Dasharatha. The bow is broken. The wedding is coming.

510.title: Two family trees
510.hook: one wedding becomes four, and two families tell their whole histories first
510.carry: gotra: a wedding joins two family lines
510.howItsDone: Hindu wedding rites include naming the gotra and ancestors of the bride's and groom's families, a custom echoed in Vasishtha's and Janaka's recitations in the Ramayana.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Janaka's bow, part three: Rama asked first, lifted it as if in play, and it broke like thunder. Your line was lila, what crushes kings is God's play.

Janaka's messengers ride hard to Ayodhya. They stand before Dasharatha, the king who not long ago begged a sage not to take his young son. Your Rama broke Shiva's bow, they tell him. Your Lakshmana is with him, safe. King Janaka asks you to come to Mithila for the wedding. You can imagine the old man's face. The next morning Dasharatha sets out with Vasishtha, his priests, his army and his treasure. When the two kings meet, Janaka welcomes him like family before they are family.
screen: `MESSENGERS RIDE TO AYODHYA.` → `YOUR RAMA BROKE SHIVA'S BOW.` → `TWO KINGS EMBRACE.`

segments.voice: Before anyone marries, the families recite their family trees, aloud, all the way back. Vasishtha names the line of Ikshvaku, generation after generation: from Brahma, through Manu, Ikshvaku himself, kings like Sagara, whose sons dug deep into the earth, and Bhagiratha, who brought the Ganga down from heaven, all the way to Dasharatha. Then Janaka names his own line from King Nimi down, including Devarata, who received the bow. Why? Because in Hindu teaching vivaha, marriage, is a samskara, one of the sacred rites that mark a life, and it doesn't join two people only. It joins two lines. Hindu families still do this. Many know their gotra, the family line traced back to an ancient sage, a rishi, like Vasishtha himself or Bharadvaja. At many weddings the priest calls out both families' gotras and ancestors before the vows. Then Janaka makes the formal gift: Sita to Rama, and his second daughter, Urmila, to Lakshmana. And then a lovely thing happens. Vishvamitra and Vasishtha together suggest something more. Janaka's younger brother, Kushadhvaja, has two daughters too, Mandavi and Shrutakirti. Why not give them to Bharata and Shatrughna? Janaka agrees with joy. So one wedding becomes four: four brothers, four brides, two royal houses woven together in a single day. Before the ceremony, Dasharatha gives away an enormous gift of cows in his sons' names. From now on, whatever happens in Ayodhya happens to Mithila too.

511.title: Companions in dharma
511.hook: a father puts his daughter's hand in a young man's hand and says one sentence
511.carry: companion in dharma: walking the path together
511.howItsDone: In Hindu weddings, the kanyadana, the father's giving of the bride's hand, and the circling of the sacred fire are central rites; some families recall Janaka's words to Rama when they explain them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, vivaha: two family trees recited aloud, and one wedding became four. Your line was gotra, a wedding joins two family lines.

If you've been to a Hindu wedding, you may know the moment, though customs vary from family to family. The fire is lit in the middle of the canopy. The priest is chanting. The bride's father stands, takes his daughter's hand, and places it in the groom's hand. Rooms full of noisy relatives go quiet for it. That moment has an echo in the Ramayana. Janaka, the king who found his daughter in a furrow, brings Sita to the altar, decked in jewels, and stands her across from Rama, by the fire.
screen: `THE FIRE UNDER THE CANOPY.` → `A FATHER, A HAND, A HAND.` → `JANAKA BRINGS SITA TO THE ALTAR.`

segments.voice: Janaka speaks to Rama: iyam sita mama suta sahadharmachari tava. This is Sita, my daughter, your companion in dharma. Accept her. Take her hand in yours. She will be devoted to you, and follow you always, like your shadow. He pours sacred water, and the gods say well done. Sahadharmachari is the key word. Saha, together. Dharma, the right way, duty, the path. Chari, one who walks. One who walks the path of dharma together with you. Not a possession, not a prize, though she was won by strength: a companion on the way. That's the Hindu teaching of marriage in one word. Janaka gives Urmila to Lakshmana, and his brother's daughters to Bharata and Shatrughna, with similar words. Then the four couples circle the fire three times, keeping it on their right. In a Hindu wedding the fire, Agni, is the witness; the vows are made in front of it. Flowers fall from the sky, heavenly drums sound, and the apsaras dance. The next morning Vishvamitra says goodbye and leaves for the northern mountains. Now the week, from the top. Ahalya's penance, and the way back. Two princes at her feet. Sita, daughter of the earth. The kings' wounded ego, and a bow lifted as if in play. Two family lines named aloud. And today, four couples circling one fire, each pair walking dharma side by side.
screen: `THIS IS SITA, MY DAUGHTER.` · `SAHADHARMACHARI: WALKING TOGETHER.` · `AGNI, THE WITNESS.` · `THE WEEK, FROM THE TOP.` · then, large: `IYAṂ SĪTĀ MAMA SUTĀ SAHADHARMACARĪ TAVA.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who walks some part of your path with you, a partner, a friend, a sibling, a colleague, and picture them beside you, not ahead or behind. On each breath in, feel their company; on each breath out, offer them yours, and if you pray, hold them in prayer.

Your line: companion in dharma, walking the path together. Not a possession, not a prize. And that's the week.
